utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Wednesday, 2nd of December, 2009. I'll first greet the witness, General Filipovic, the accused, the Defence counsel. Good afternoon, Mr. Scott and all your team, and the people assisting us. Mr. Registrar, you have one IC number for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Thank you. 2D has submitted a response to the Prosecution's objections to their requests to the admission of documents tendered through Witness 4D-AB. This list shall be given Exhibit IC01140. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Before I give the floor to the Defence teams for their cross-examination, just a short administrative reminder. We'll have just one break tomorrow, and we will finish at 6.00 p.m. We might be finished by then. If we aren't, the witness will return on Monday. Regarding next week, we know that we're going to have a witness who's scheduled for next week. The Defence should have two hours for their examination-in-chief and re-direct. As for the other Defence teams, they will have one hour, and the Prosecutor will have two hours. Next week, we'll have three days, Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday. We're not sitting on Thursday because there's the Judges' plenary meeting on Thursday. This was by way of a reminder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you're now into a new stage of the proceedings. You're going to answer questions by the other Defence teams. Thereafter, the Prosecutor, Prosecutor Scott, sitting on your right-hand side, will have questions for you. I know that you are very familiar with cross-examination, because back in April 2009 -- or nearly nine years ago, you were cross-examined by Mr. Nice back then. So to avoid any problem, if a question is asked of you, listen to the question and then answer very freely. If you don't like the question - that may happen - you then answer the question. Most of the time, the Prosecutor will try to elicit a "yes" or a "no" from you. And if he has additional questions, well, he'll put them to you, because he's the one conducting the cross-examination. But it may happen that you do not like the questions put to you because, of course, the Prosecutor is trying to argue his case and will ask questions along his lines, just as was done by the Defence for their own case. You may agree with the Prosecutor, but you also may disagree with him. If you do not agree with him, don't get angry about it. He's doing his job. So this is what I wanted to tell you so that you understand the type of system we work in. In your country, your domestic system is very different. Judges put questions as I am used to doing it. You know, I'm not in favour of one case or the other. When I put questions and when my fellow Judges put questions, we just put comprehensive questions. But here each side has its own point of view, and it may be that the Prosecutor's view is not yours. You must understand that. That's the rule of the game. But I think you understood, because I saw that in the Kordic case there was no incident in the proceedings. You answered well. But I just wanted to preempt any problem. Therefore, without further adieu, I shall give the floor to Ms. Nozica. She's ready, she has the lectern already, she has her documents. She's ready to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honours, and everybody else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to you, Mr. Filipovic. I'd just like to check whether the usher has the documents I want Mr. Filipovic to look at. Yes, the witness does, too, yes. Fine. Now, Mr. Filipovic, for your benefit and everybody else's here in the courtroom, I'd like to emphasise that during my cross-examination I'm going to be asking you about three topics. The first relates to January 1993 and the events that took place at the time, and that is how the corridor in Busovaca was cut off, and there was a lot about that during the examination-in-chief. The next topic will deal with April 1993 in Central Bosnia, and the third area will be the events in June 1993 after the signed agreement in Kiseljak. Now, to be as efficacious as possible, let's start off with the first document in my binder, because I'm sure that you haven't seen most of these documents before, or maybe you have. The first is 2D3068. Mr. Filipovic, you'll find that they're set out in the order I'm going to take them. So this is a report signed by Ignjac Kostroman, Tihomir Blaskic, Dario Kordic, and Anto Valenta. It is a report of the 26th of January, 1993. It says here that: "Open and brutal aggression by strong Muslim forces is continuing from the direction of Zenica towards Busovaca, Vitez, Travnik, Novi Travnik, and Kiseljak ..." Now, Mr. Filipovic, these next few documents will refer to the cutting off of the corridor, and I'd like to stress that you indicated this to us yesterday on the map, and then the maps have received IC numbers, 01337 is the first, and 1138. It says here that all this is done with the objective to completely destroy the HVO and the Croatian people on the territory of Central Bosnia. Croatian villages are being burnt down, along with churches and other monuments of culture of the Croatian people. It goes on to say that this is an open aggression by more powerful forces, and then there's a piece of information here which I'm going to ask you about, whether you knew about this. Five mountain brigades were sent on Busovaca, and the city is being fired at from all directions, and that the Mujahedins and Green Legion, and other extremist formations, are first when it comes to slaughter. At the same time, Television Sarajevo is leading a brutal campaign and propaganda. And then under item 2, it says: "Our forces are quite stretched and cut off between municipalities because they are holding the line towards the Chetniks, 70 per cent of its length, and now general mobilisation has been conducted in order to protect the Croatian people from the slaughterers. So far, the village of Dusina has been completely burned down, mixed and only Croatian houses; they are slaughtering women, children, and the elderly, and for the moment we do not have any reliable information on the number killed." Then it goes on to make three -- list three requests: First of all, requesting immediate help in MTS and manpower, and that the public needs to be urgently informed about the massacre in the Lasva region; then under B, aid and ammunition; and then finally it says: "You should know that every one of our people who was massacred and slaughtered was killed by the Muslim forces." Now, Mr. Filipovic, are you familiar with the data contained in this report, and can you confirm that the report for this day and for that period is correct and that the facts there set out are correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know the facts, and I know what the situation was like in that general area, but I also know that the emphasis was on Busovaca. This, to a certain extent -- not for this particular day, because we have a date there, but this is, in fact, a report for the past seven or ten days, and we were most hard hit by the fact that, for example, from the Lasva Valley we couldn't pass through to Busovaca because there was this obstacle at Ahmici. And what is also important for Busovaca is that the road towards Kiseljak was cut off at Kacuni and Bilalovac, which means that, well, the signature of these four men here who had this information, well, Blaskic reported about the conflict even before this, but they wanted to -- the document to have greater weight with these four signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Excuse me, Counsel. I'm sure the counsel can identify for us some basis, but nonetheless for purposes of the record, Your Honour, since this went on quite extensively yesterday as well, I wonder if counsel might inform us what relevance this has, other than tu quoque.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I can inform you about. My learned friend shows some documents, and these documents support her thesis, and I consider them to be extremely important, particularly these reports that came in from the HVO, because my learned friend, first of all, based herself on the documents -- based what she had to say on BH Army documents, and I'd like us to check out and verify to see whether the reports that were coming in from the HVO were true and correct, with the proviso that I'm not going to just base myself on HVO reports, but will also base my case on reports sent out by the international community about these individual points. I also refer to point 31, or, rather, paragraph 31 of the indictment, and I do think that this is important and relevant, and, first and foremost, that it is linked to the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, but with due respect to my friend, the fact that she considers them important is really not a basis. I consider a lot of things important, myself, but that doesn't necessarily mean it's relevant to the courtroom. There's still no articulated basis as to how this is relevant, anything other than tu quoque. So my objection continues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will render an oral ruling on these issues tomorrow, when we start the hearing, and it will solve the problem. Whatever the case may be, please proceed, Ms. Nozica. At any rate, Mr. Scott, under item 3 in this document, it might be interesting about the international armed conflict, about your case, about the fact that the Republic of Croatia can make a contribution in MTS and in troops as well, so this document is at the very heart of all our discussions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, as I feel that this is a comment to my part of the examination-in-chief, I would like to indicate, as Ms. Nozica has already said, paragraph 31 of the indictment, in which Busovaca is explicitly mentioned, and it is mentioned in the following context: that on the 15th of January, when the ultimatum expired, around that time the HVO took military and violent actions to enforce the ultimatum, attacking and pressing the Muslims at a number of locations, including at Novi Travnik, Gornji Vakuf, and Busovaca. Therefore, what we're trying to prove here, in relation to Busovaca and the cutting off of the corridor, is directly linked to paragraph 31 of the indictment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, take a look at the next document, which is 2D3069. It's the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. General, I'm not really addressing the substance of this document. I'm really surprised by the fact that we see Mr. Blaskic's signature. It is co-signed by three main figures; Kostroman, Valenta, and Kordic. I see also that this is an extremely urgent dispatch to Mr. Tudjman, to the HVO commander in the forward command post, to the head of the Defence Department, and also to the Chief of Staff. So upon reading this document, my impression - and you will tell me yours - my impression is Mr. Blaskic is bypassing his own chain of command, exerts pressure on Mr. Tudjman for him to take action by sending MTS, soldiers, to the Lasva Valley area. If I were Mr. Mate Boban, if I were the Chief of Staff, if I were the head of the Defence Department, if I were Mr. Prlic, in the very few seconds that follow I would relieve Mr. Blaskic of his position, because he did not respect the chain of command. Now, how do you account for this being possible? How could this be done at the time? How could a commander, such as Mr. Blaskic, allow himself to directly address a foreign head of state, with all the political problems that it involves, without going through his chain of command? Let me take an example. Let us imagine today that the American commander, McChrystal in Afghanistan, directly goes to Mr. Brown, the British prime minister. Everybody would find that absolutely abnormal. So how could such a thing happen in your country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in a sense, this is a cry for help. They are intensively seeking assistance. Herceg-Bosna, or Mate Boban, or Prlic, do not have the possibility of offering that assistance by reporting on these events. There's no television, there are no newspapers. And Tudjman can do that. That's one point. Secondly, there was precedent. You mentioned the American commander in Afghanistan. I remember from some memoirs that Eisenhower addressed Stalin with some questions, and then Churchill was angry why Eisenhower went directly to Stalin. But when it's a matter of life or death, you choose the means you can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your answer is to say that it was the situation, at the time there was grave danger, you so say so he went directly to Tudjman. Very well, thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, an additional question. Do you remember where Mr. Boban and the leadership of the HZ-HB on the 26th of January were located? Where were they? Were they perhaps in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps that was the reason, but I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, I ask you to look at the next document, which is 2D3069. You said a moment ago that Mr. Blaskic signed reports himself, alone, and you also said -- you also mentioned the cutting off of the corridor at Kacuni, so let's look at this report which is as of the same day as the previous one. We can see who it was sent to. There's no need to dwell on that. And then he goes on to say: "Open and brutal aggression which has been in preparation for some time against HVO formations, and it began with extremely furious attacks by the Muslim forces who, on the 24th of January, 1993, in the afternoon hours, erected a barricade at a previously designated place called Kacuni, near Busovaca, and stopped five vehicles (tanks), the UN, and a regular military police patrol vehicle. They fired a rocket-launcher and opened intense fire from infantry weapons, thereby wounding the deputy commander of the military police of the HVO of Busovaca, Mr. Ivo Perovic, in the leg, wounded in the leg, who, after brutal torture, was slaughtered." His neck was slit. And then it says that a taxi-driver came to his assistance, who was also wounded on the occasion. Now, further down, paragraph 3, it says that for the execution of this task given to the BH Army, the enemy withdrew forces from the battle-fields at Visoko, Ilijas, Maglaj, and Zavidovici and infiltrated the Mujahedins there -- inserted the Mujahedins. Then it goes on to speak about "our forces," meaning the HVO. And then just like in the previous document, it says that the line has been extended facing the Chetniks. And there's mention of losses sustained. Now, you said that the intention of the BH Army was that the strong forces on the other side were grouped from Zenica, Perin Han, Drivusa, Dusina, Lugovi, Kacuni, Zivcici, Pridol, Zenica-Kaonik, Zenica-Vjetrenica, and Zenica-Han Bila, with the object of completely cutting off Busovaca and Kiseljak and destroying the HVO in the Lasva region. Now, this document has more purely military information, although it's similar to the previous document that we looked at. Both these documents are dated the 26th of January. One arrived, as we can see look, looking at the stamp, it reached the Main Staff at 0820 hours, and this one arrived at 0332 hours. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber, or, rather, confirm -- or do these two documents confirm what you are saying, that Mr. Blaskic sent information to the HZ-HB and that the first document we looked at is a cry for help? Could we put it that way?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a purely military document. There's no doubt about it, that it was drafted by Blaskic, although I think that drafting of the document signed by the other persons was done by the same hand, but in this document it's more elaborated. All the events are correctly stated, except for maybe the assessment of the Muslim forces. When he says "five brigades," well, then this issue of -- in how large an area. There could have been more or less if we talk about -- strictly about Busovaca itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us what the abbreviation "RIR" at the beginning of the list of addressees refers to, what it means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Urgent, urgent, urgent." We are probably in the mode of transmission, or maybe a code. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. You have spoken of signatures. This document is not signed. The copy I have, I do not see a signature. Did you find one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no signature on my copy, either, but I can confirm its authenticity. Knowing Blaskic, I can confirm that he was the author.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's conclusive that this was relayed through a packet radio service.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you recognise the style or the signature, because there's no signature?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The style, the thought processes behind this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's take a look at another document, the next, 2D3067. This is a consolidated report by Mr. Petkovic, dated 27th of January, 1993. Please take a look at item 2, referring to Central Bosnia. Have you found that? That's on page 2 in the Croatian version, item 2, "Central Bosnia." Let's take a look at the report from Vitez at 1600 hours. It states -- well, Chetniks, we will skip that. That's not important: "Muslims." During the morning hours, a strong offensive began from the direction Zenica-Lasva-Dusina. According to estimates, Busovaca is being attacked by about 8500 enemy soldiers, and also observed were tank movements from Kakanj and Zenica. Then we have another report from 2020 hours. Then, on the next page, there is the midnight report, and it states there -- I'm showing you because of the IC marks that you made on the map, that IC01137 and IC11138 that you made on the maps. It says here at 2400 hours: "The situation in the responsibility zone of the Brigade Zrinski-Busovaca is as follows. After the brutal aggression of the Muslim forces from the direction of Zenica-Lasva-Dusina and Kacuni to Lugovi, during afternoon hours a front-line was established on the line Kuber (Saracevac elevation 957) to Putis, Grablje, Merdani, Dusina, Nezidovici" -- those place are not reflected in the transcript, but it doesn't matter. We will rectify that later on. Continuing: " ... Nezidovici, Proscica, Kacuni, Modrikamen, Pridolci, Luske Staje, Busovaca Staje, and Rovna." And it follows: "During the day, Muslim forces brought in fresh forces from the direction of Zenica with the objective to strengthen the corridor Lasva-Dusine-Kacuni and connect between Lugova and Fojnica whereby they would be cutting off Busovaca from Kiseljak and make it impossible to use the road Kiseljak-Busovaca." Mr. Filipovic, does this document confirm your reference to the cutting off and the blockade that was effected those days Busovaca in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, that Chetniks are mentioned together with Muslims in such reports. Up to that point, Busovaca was not at war, because it was deeper within our territory with respect to the front-line towards the Chetniks, but now we see all those place names, and the HVO cannot leave from Busovaca neither towards Kiseljak nor towards Vitez. For at least 10 to 15 days, Busovaca was completely encircled and had to fend for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now let's take a look at P1349. It is a Cheshire Regiment report - this would be the next document in your binder - dated the 23rd of January, 1993. It states here that it covers the period from the 9th to 29th, but since we have a different date here, I just focused on that. It reads that a liaison officer team visited Mr. Commander Nikola Jazinovic. He was a commander of the HVO in Busovaca. Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that person. He commanded the unit at Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Further on, it states in the report that in communication with him, under A and B on page 1, that the HVO intercepted two fax messages, one purportedly signed by the 3rd Corps commander, dated 16th of January, asking for more manpower and reinforcement and munition replenishment for the BiH forces in the Kacuni area until victory was achieved, and another fax from -- dated 28th of January stating that all HVO prisoners were to be taken to Zenica and that the BiH Army were to collect and bury all Croat bodies from the villages of Nezirovici and Gusti Grab. This is what Mr. Jazinovic said to the liaison officer of the Cheshire Regiment Battalion. It states here that BiH Army attacked and destroyed the following Croat villages, and Jazinovic thinks Muslim extremists and the BH Army killed 12 old people at Dusine, that they took another 30 people, that both Catholic churches at Dusine and Proscica had been destroyed. The author of the document said they found the village of Prosje, as they understood it to be named. And Jazinovic said that the HVO's goal was to continue active defence of the front-line around Busovaca. Then further on, it says Jazinovic stated that there were a number of incidents "last week" on the 23rd of January. Sixteen HVO soldiers who were on reconnaissance, commanded by Vlado Kriste. They were captured at Kacuni. Then it makes reference to the 24th of January event when a BH Army soldier hit a military policeman from HVO, that Mile Rasic was killed during negotiations. I'm going to go quickly through this. Please turn to page 4, and that would be 0027-4361 in the English version. It discusses the situation at Vitez, and in the last paragraph of item 3, which refers to Vitez, it says: "We received samples of infantry weapons ammunition produced in the Middle East. A reliable source told us that such ammunition reaches the Muslim parts of Vitez via Muslim humanitarian food aid ..." But this is no longer related reports coming from Mr. Jazinovic. It would be a report sourced from the Cheshire Battalion. And then the next paragraph is also important: "Receive information that members of the Visoko Brigade of the BiH Army took part in blowing up a bridge, thereby cutting off the road between Kacuni and Kiseljak." It stated that the bridge is not completely destroyed, that it's still passable. And, finally, let's take a look at page 7 in your version, and that would be the English version 0027-4363, with respect to Travnik. We received this document from the Prosecution. And referring to Travnik, it says: "The body of the two Britons ..." Have you found this page?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just found out that I have a document in my own language.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You are always provided with a version in your language. "The bodies of the two Britons executed south of Travnik two days ago have been recovered back to Zenica." Today, on the 5th of February, 1993 -- it refers to medical workers who were killed in the well-known stronghold of extremist Muslims. It's stated here that on the 5th of February, they were examined by a pathologist. Marks on both bodies indicated that the men had been kneeling, with hands tied behind their back, when they were shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, such facts should be somewhat linked to crimes alleged in the indictment, and where with these murder of British soldiers, I fail to find any tie. I think it's a bit far-fetched now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I haven't gone too far. I mentioned this detail because this item refers to the 5th of February, 1993. Let's make matters clear. The whole document is dated - I wanted to be clear-cut about it - is dated 29th of January 1993. But since the reference that is made to the murder of those two British persons is the 5th of February, the only conclusion I can draw is that this is a consolidated report. I wanted to highlight that from the start so that there would be no doubt as to the nature of this document. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would advise you to come a bit closer to the facts alleged in the indictment. And what you're telling me about the dates I find strange, really. Do you think that the document --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, I'll try to explain. The whole document, except for the last paragraph, refers to events prior to the 29th of January. The last inclusions, under 4 in Travnik, make reference to events taking place on the 5th of February, 1993, which lead you to a conclusion that the whole report was drafted on the 5th of February. And to make sure that there is no confusion as to the dates, I highlighted that, and I'm quite clear and close to what the witness knows and what is the matter at hand, except for that last reference which is dated the 5th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Please do not misunderstand me. I do not think you are misleading. I think this document is simply contradictory. That's it. There's no way around that. This document is quite contradictory, and I don't think neither you, nor I, nor the witness can explain why. But please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let's try to resolve this through the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, you had all the information that I related from this document to you, the information provided by Mr. Jazinovic, that information on BiH Army attacks concerning the village of Dusina, what happened in Vitez, what I read to you about those events, and at Visoko, that they blew up the bridge. I'm going to ask you about the information relating to Central Bosnia towards the end of January 1993. Can you confirm for us that all these events did really happen?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Mr. Jazinovic, Nikola Jazinovic, who was the commander of the brigade in Busovaca, but he did not hail from Busovaca - he came from another part of Bosnia - he was one of the most professional people, one of the best we had available in the area of responsibility of our operations zone. This document relates his reports, that which he conveyed to the Cheshire Battalion, and I know about those events to be true. Furthermore, the area south-east of Travnik is the Bila River Valley, which was a stronghold of the Mujahedin and where Sefer established the Patriotic League, meaning the Han Bila area, but the sequence of place names, the villages, it makes reference to all the significant events during that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. We are closing this chapter on January --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I still want to know what the murder of these British soldiers has to do with our case. You have not given the slightest answer to that question of mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the answer to your question in relation to this document of the Cheshire Battalion, it confirms everything that was previously shown in documents of the BH Army and the HVO about what was going on in Central Bosnia in the days before this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you please indicate where the murder of these two British was mentioned before? And this still does not mean that it's relevant. I think this is a detail which really goes beyond anything that you can claim, in behaviour of the Muslims, to have something to do with this case, frankly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm going to explain this for the fourth time. It doesn't have anything to do with that, and I just showed it because of the date of the document. But I didn't ask the witness to confirm the events at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, you did, you did ask him to confirm the events. And he did, actually. But okay, we leave it at that. I'm not convinced that this is relevant, but please go on, because the purpose is not to lose time. So I'm not insisting in a further discussion on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we've lost quite a bit of time, so I will ask another question to determine this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, when you said that you knew the place names, the situation mentioned in this document, did you include there or exclude the event that relates to the killing of these two humanitarian workers? And I didn't ask you anything about that myself.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I included it, and it's all linked together, spilling over in a narrow area and in the broader area.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Now look at P9008, the next document. It's a statement of yours. We have to hurry up a bit now. And it was given on the 10th. Would you take a look at this next document. It says: "Major General Filip Filipovic, retired," personal information, and it lists various topics. The document was compiled on the 10th of April, 2000. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what this is all about?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This should be a document prepared for the trial in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Will you tell us which trial, for the record?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kordic trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Does this statement contain information that you provided?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not to read it all now, I think that they were the pages that were sent through Naumovski in the Kordic trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm just going to focus on certain points, such as point 29 in this statement. You have the Croatian version, I believe, and it refers to the distribution of weapons at the beginning of the conflict with the Serbs. And then point 34, 35, and 36, which refers to the 7th Muslim Brigade, and you've mentioned that here; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You spoke about it in an almost identical fashion. And then paragraph 44, about the Easter celebrations in Travnik, and you spoke about that here, too. So this document, for the most part, confirms your statements and testimony here. You weren't asked some things at the time, and you weren't asked some things here during the examination-in-chief. But can we just go to April 1996 -- I mean 1993. I beg your pardon. And we'll skip one document and go on to 2D1468.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: 1486. You're quite right. This is a statement for the public, coming from the Information Department for Central Bosnia, and it says: "Yesterday, the terrorists, the Mujahedin in Novi Travnik, kidnapped Miro Jerkovic, a driver, Vlado Sliskovic, Zdravko Kovacevic [as interpreted], Ivica Kambic, all officers of the HVO, and the bandits took away the HVO members towards Ravno Rostovo." The date is the 14th of April, 1993. And then the next paragraph says: "Last night, members of the Muslim military attempted another terrorist act against Kruscica, Vitez." And then the next paragraph: "The public has already been informed about the horrendous murder of Mirak, Stjepica ..." And then it goes on to speak about the attacks on members of the Kotromanic Brigade, and says at the bottom, since this is a public information, "the HVO message is clear, we do not want a conflict with the Muslim Army. We want the Vance-Owen Plan to be implemented, which was signed by our President, Mate Boban, and by the Muslim president, Alija Izetbegovic, we want peace," written in capital letters, "and if the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina continues, we want a joint front against the aggressor, the Chetniks. However, it is the holy duty of the HVO to protect its soldiers, all Croats, and all citizens living in the Croatian provinces, and the HVO is capable of doing that. "That is why we entreat the BH Army to immediately deal with their terrorists and extremists, or the HVO is going to do it, efficiently and completely." Now, Mr. Filipovic, tell me, first, do you remember this public announcement, and were these the positions of the HVO in Central Bosnia with respect to the conflict with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a lot of my own style here, and this was sent out through Jadranko Topic -- Ilija Topic -- Topic? Yes, this is correct, but in that last part here we emphasised that it was the Mujahedin's fault. We didn't want all Muslims to be against us, because we were ultimately weaker, so there are a lot of my thoughts and words in the composition of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, you're using figurative speech, so could you explain?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it went through the Press Centre, but I don't know if I dictated some of this, but a lot of the wording and the kind of style I use is to be found here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, your time is up, your 30 minutes are up. But you can have some additional time, since the two hours allotted to the Defence teams were not fully used by everyone. Witness, before I give the floor back to Ms. Nozica, I have a question for you. I'm looking at this document, 2D1486, and I read that these Mujahedins seem to be a cause for conflict between the BH Army and the HVO; i.e., if they weren't there, there wouldn't be so many problems. This document shows that they did several things against Jerkovic, and there's also an attack against Kraljevic, and it says that they are definitely fueling the conflict between the HVO and the BH Army. I'm quite interested, because I'd like to know whether the Prosecutor's case is right or whether the Defence's case is right, and whether this was really the reason for the conflict that occurred between the HVO and the BH Army. Now, you were in the field at the time, so do you believe that this reflects the reality, that the words used in this document reflect the reality? In this document, it says that the Vance-Owen Plan exists, that one can think what they want about it, but it does exist. It says that Mate Boban and Izetbegovic both want peace, but that the Mujahedin are playing a role. Now, what's your take on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reason for the conflict was certainly not the Mujahedin. They were a component part of the overall situation in the territory, but they were something quite different, compared to the civilisation and history and situation in the area up until then. That's all I want to say about the Mujahedin. I don't wish to say any more, because there were about 1500 of them, but they were burgeoning and their numbers grew because the extremist elements in the population joined them. Now, the conflict in the Lasva Valley was, in my opinion, due to unresolved questions relating to the survival of people in the area and the large number of refugees that were coming into the area. It was becoming more populated. Villages became mixed. People were coming into these mixed villages who had never lived there before, so this gave rise to problems and conflicts. And the whole war was a war of separation, division, distribution, partitioning, so that each part endeavoured to find ways and means of making a livelihood for themselves and seeking out a place for themselves in the territory. The Serbs took my heritage, the land of my forefathers, up at Vlasic, for instance, and the people of Travnik lived on the basis of what that area produced for centuries. And now you have all these refugees coming in. So I don't want to say that the Mujahedin were to blame for everything, although without doubt they were a decisive factor in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. I apologise, Your Honours, but to avoid any misunderstanding with regard to the allotment of time, I said yesterday that the Coric Defence, according to the situation as it was yesterday, would probably not have any cross-examination. However, a few moments ago the Stojic Defence showed a statement of the witness given in the Kordic case. P09008 is the number. Now, in view of the contents of that statement, and if it is admitted into evidence as an exhibit, then Mr. Coric and I are going to conduct -- or, rather, I'm going to conduct a cross-examination, although it will be a brief one and will probably be shorter than the 24 minutes that I have at my disposal according to the first allotment of time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll bear that in mind. And I've just informed my colleague Ms. Pinter that I will have two more documents and be done within 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Speed up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may briefly answer Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic. You can, of course, not condition your cross-examination on whether the document is admitted, because that's a decision which will be taken further on by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President -- MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am fully conscious of that. But out of an abundance of caution, I do wish to cross-examine, because I don't know what the Trial Chamber is going to decide. It might admit two paragraphs, reject the whole document, or whatever. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: While we're on the topic, Your Honour, it might be appropriate for the Prosecution to state its concerns as well. We think it's entirely inappropriate to -- if it's counsel's intention - and at the moment I can only assume that it is - to tender that statement into evidence. This is apparently an attempt to convert this witness, in part, into a 92 ter witness, with no notice to the other parties or to the Court. If that's the case, that substantially impacts the Prosecution's ability to effective cross-examination. We've now gone from -- potentially gone from Ms. Alaburic's examination, many of the topics of which in this statement were never addressed. Now, on the third day of this witness's testimony, the Prosecution is faced with the prospect that another 18 pages or so -- 14 pages are going to become part of the evidence of this witness, and we can't possibly meet that under these circumstances. So we object to the document being received at all or being further considered in this case. If the Chamber is minded to consider it, then we will ask for the witness to be brought back at such time as the Prosecution has adequate time to fully prepare its cross-examination on another 14 pages of material. This is inappropriate. If there was an intention for a party to call a witness as 92 ter, it should have been noticed, and the procedure should have been followed accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am surprised by what you say. You say the witness will have to return for you to be able to cross-examine him. I don't know how you prepare your work, but the basics in any preparation for his examination would be to read his testimony in the Kordic case. Your colleague, Mr. Nice, together with Mr. Kordic's counsel, when they put questions to the witness, they put it based on this document, and they tackled each and every paragraph of it. Earlier on, when I saw this document, I saw paragraph 4 and I thought, oh, Mr. Coric might have something to say to this. It doesn't take hours or days or months to understand a document, especially four years into the trial. I mean, you are competent enough to face any topic whatsoever. If not, that's a problem. So at any rate, we were not dealing with the whole document. Ms. Nozica only had a few questions on it, and Mr. Coric's lawyer wants to address paragraph 40. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that's -- I'll start with the last statement. That's not really correct. Counsel didn't put a single question to the witness about the statement, except to say, Is that your statement? Which would be a 92 ter type of question. There wasn't a single question to the witness on the content of the statement. Now, Your Honour, I appreciate your compliments on my competence as a counsel. I hope that's the case. But be that as it may, and there is a procedure, there are rules to be followed, and it cannot be the answer to every breach of a rule to say, Well, too bad, you can deal with it yourself. Let's -- too bad. That's not the issue. There is a proper procedure for tendering 92 ter evidence. It has not been followed in this case. I do prepare. I'll match my hours in the last 10 days preparing this witness to anyone in the courtroom, the nights and the weekends that I've spent here, but I prepared to meet the evidence of this witness and the cross and the direct examinations that are conducted. Ms. Alaburic completed her direct examination yesterday. The topics that she didn't cover, some of those that I may have been aware of, I did not -- have not pursued further on that basis. And this is inappropriate. And yes, I'm confident, I think so, but I object to any procedure by where any Prosecution counsel is put into a position or has to deal with this evidence in this way. It's not appropriate, it's not fair, it shouldn't be allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is now on record. Yes, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow me to say a couple of words. Immediately as Madam Nozica showed this document, I stated that it was a witness statement. I wanted to suggest to her that this is not a witness statement. This is a document prepared by Mr. Kordic's Defence counsel, who was supposed to be the basis for the examination of this witness in the Kordic case. It is a fact that the English text of this document has been verified and authenticated by this witness, but this is not a witness statement. These are the wordings of Mr. Kordic's Defence counsel. So in a certain way, I would support part of my learned friend Scott's discussion regarding this document. Another thing I'd like to say is that I find it quite questionable that one Defence team cross-examines because another Defence team broaches an issue or shows a document. If we permit that, then in this courtroom expect very strange games, to the detriment of certain Defence teams, and we shouldn't allow this to be a principle of conduct. Thirdly, even if this document is put forward by the Stojic Defence team for admission, since it's been the practice of this trial that portions of documents be admitted that were discussed with the witness, I'd like to point your attention to the fact that Madam Nozica directed the witness towards paragraphs 29, 34 to 36, and 44. Therefore, paragraph 40 has not been mentioned here. And the broaching of the issue of military police in Central Bosnia may be interesting if the Court allows. We are going to deal with that in our redirect. But this is, indeed, a new issue being broached, and if Mr. Scott deems that he should need some time to prepare to discuss this subject, I would support his claim for that. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I may have misunderstood my learned colleague, but I'm not playing any games in this courtroom. And the principle, whereby cross-examination is allowed for issues opened or broached by other Defence teams, has been confirmed in this trial for several times. We've been doing that for a long time, and I'm not making a precedent here. I do not have any intention to broach the subject of military police there, and if I were to be guaranteed by the Bench that this is not going to be admitted, meaning paragraph 40 and 41, are not going to be admitted, then I would not cross-examine and I would not object to that. But at this point, I do not have any guarantees that this will not be admitted, so it is my duty to defend Mr. Coric's interests and cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I interrupt?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to slow down and speak one at a time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will cut this unnecessary discussion short. I'm not going to propose this document be admitted. I'm not going to propose its admittance, but I'm truly surprised that the Prosecution is reacting to their own document. This is the Prosecutor's document. I'm not going to seek admittance, because this was meant to be just a reminder of the issues that the witness is going to be examined upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your kind co-operation. This solves the problems. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, some 15 minutes ago, when discussing 2D1486 [as interpreted], we discussed -- and that is the press release - you do not have to seek for that document - at the end of that document it is stated: "We ask the BiH Army to get rid of their terrorists and extremists; otherwise, the HVO is going to do that." So we're not discussing the Mujahedin, but you spoke about extremists in the ranks of the BiH Army. Were there those who wanted to instigate conflicts with the Croats and there were others who wanted a peaceful solution in Bosnia-Herzegovina; am I right in saying so?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to intervene. On page 12, line 20 in the transcript, the number of the document is incorrect. The correct number is 2D3067. Just an intervention in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So concerning this issue that we've broached, please take a look at 2D686. That would be the next document in the binder. It's a document signed by Mr. Stjepan Siber, deputy commander of the Staff of the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You know that gentleman?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This document is addressed to the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, commander of the Staff of the Supreme Command of the Army, and let me remind you - maybe unnecessarily, maybe you recall all that - this document was created after the Kiseljak agreement dated the 10th of June, and Madam Alaburic showed this agreement under P2726. You said that there was a replacement of the commander of the Staff of the Supreme Command of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a replacement was made.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is an exhibit, so we're not going to go through this whole document. Mr. Siber is sending a message whereby he discusses the situation in Zenica of the time, and you, yourself, said that this agreement was never honoured and that the real intense fighting started after that, initiated by the BiH Army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So it's stated here that on the 25th of June, it was spoken [as interpreted] with the representative of the municipal authorities in Zenica, and that he, in front of Karadzic, Franjic, and him, he said that as a citizen he was disappointed with the leadership of the 3rd Corps because they were implicated in looting and crime. It says there are officers who execute people after looting. In item 2 in this document, it says that on the 23rd of June, there was a meeting with Hodzic and Karadzic, the president of the District Government of Zenica, and it reads: "Merdan is the main organiser of religious units of Cuvalic's and of Puric's." And then we come to the most salient point. It says that: "Zenica and the 3rd Corps units are led by people who are hardened criminals, who do not want, because it doesn't serve their purposes, to defeat the Chetniks, but conflicts with the HVO play into their hand." The next document discusses the shooting of 50 civilians. That would be the last paragraph of the document. The shooting of 50 civilians was done by the Mujahedin, dated the 26th of February. And, finally, Mr. Siber proposes that instead of Merdan, somebody of the same profile as Negovetic, Karadzic, should be appointed to the joint command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, but I -- we just read a document linked and then there was no question. I mean, that's even taking all this even a step further. We at least, sometimes, go through the charade of asking a real question at the end of a long reading, but now we're not even doing that. We just read the document and then go on and start reading the next document. I really don't see the relevance of all this. I know the Chamber said it will issue some sort of a ruling tomorrow. That won't do us a whole lot of good right now. If this isn't tu quoque, counsel should have to articulate -- with great respect, counsel should articulate to the Chamber a basis why this is relevant other than tu quoque on something in the indictment. The fact that Busovaca -- Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm going to finish my submission. The fact that Busovaca is mentioned in the indictment, doesn't just simply make everything that mentions Busovaca relevant. And we've spent an hour now reading documents. I've never seen anything like it in my life, and I've been practicing for 30 years. I've never seen anything like this. What is the possible value of this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you had better do as I do. Look at other proceedings and see how your colleagues go about it. Sometimes they read documents for a long time and then they ask questions, and that's what she's doing. She reads the document that the witness may know or may not know, and then there will be a question. And I'm really anxious to hear the question, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would have had an opportunity to meet the witness, and I would have proofed him, but I did not have that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So, finally, my question: Does it follow from this document that the deputy commander of the Staff of the Supreme Command, Mr. Siber, confirms exactly what you discussed in your examination-in-chief, in your testimony, that in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina there are extremists who -- as it's stated here, who cause the conflicts with the HVO in Zenica, for instance? And the date is very important because it covers May and June, as can be divined from the date.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Siber, in my opinion, was on the other side, but I would kiss him on the cheek for this document, because I know the persons who are being referred to; Merdan, for instance, Vran, Haracic. I know of the incidents which happened around this date in terms of the horrible crime at Bikosi, and that's between Han Bila and Guca Gora. On the 10th, I came to this area being referred to here and felt the difficulties caused by those instigators of conflict that are named by Siber in this document. What is -- it is relevant for the events and the timing of those events within the area of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in the Kordic case the Prosecutor, Mr. Nice, had asked you why you had not joined the BH Army, which was the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he gave you the case of Colonel Siber, which is mentioned here, too. And your answer was that you preferred to go for another solution. So this is what I remind you of. Now, upon reading this document, which has been used by the Prosecution already in another case - it is a well known exhibit, Prosecution exhibit - we have a Croat of the ABiH who here incriminates the 3rd Corps and its command, and lists all the crimes committed by the Mujahedin, who are, according to him, under Merdan, and he is now requiring for a relief of the command. So this document shows that within the ABiH, there were disagreements. And if there are disagreements of a military nature, that means that there are also political problems and dissensions among various factions. As far as you know -- we know that the HVO was wire-tapping the BH Army phone calls. A witness came to tell us so. So when the ABiH was conducting a military action against you, were they all in agreement, or was there one faction that decided to carry out an offensive because there was a specific problem, or was this an overall plan against the HVO? What is your view on this, because this document may shed some light on part of the conflict, even if the Prosecutor thinks it's not a relevant document, but that's the Prosecutor's view.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you are following the right track, but let me tell you at all times I considered myself a member of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, be it labelled "VRS," "BiH Army" or the "HVO," or any other label. I belonged to Bosnia-Herzegovina. I belonged and I will belong to it. And nobody had the right, be it HVO or anybody else, to put this in another context except for that, the context of the defence of the people who lived there. Let it be perfectly clear that I was -- I considered myself to be in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Before the war, I only used to be in Yugoslavia, but from the start of the war I was in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I gave nobody the right to put me on some other side. Of course, secondly, there were radical forces and less radical forces. In the period discussed by this document, let me tell you this: The Travnik Muslims, since we were an enclave from the 10th onwards when I came to that area, the Travnik Muslims were not killed in fighting against us. Almost none of them -- there were 30.000 Travnik Muslims, and none of them lost their lives in fighting against us. The Krajina Muslims, the Mujahedins, members of other units brought in were those casualties, but not a single Muslim from Travnik was killed in the fighting against us. And this is an illustration of the situation. When we make mention of Mujahedins, I can tell you that there was a radical understanding that Bosnia-Herzegovina is to be the way that Alija Izetbegovic says it should be, and it would not be a Bosnia-Herzegovina in which I would have a right to live and to fight for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're telling us that there was some kind of radicalisation within the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stated that on the day before yesterday. In June 1992, as early as that, there was a complete reshuffling of the personnel, leading cadre in the Lasva River Valley, from the municipal TO staffs, two commanders. I mentioned Lendo in Novi Travnik, I think, or in Travnik, rather. Then Alagic shows up and others, with all due respect to all of those that I name, they were, professionally, working towards the interests of their own people, but that was not a policy, or the way of life, or the civilisation that I was used to and that I had grown up in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will look at the last document I wanted to deal with precisely on the topic you had raised.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may we correct something in line 17. The witness said it was not the policy, so the "not" is missing there. Or could you tell us, Witness, was it or wasn't it a policy? Did you say it was or wasn't?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was talking about the Muslims, and the way in which it was implemented was not the policy as it was while I was growing up and living there and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So, Mr. Filipovic, following on from the questions asked you by Judge Antonetti today, and we started broaching the topic yesterday towards the end of your testimony, let's see what the political framework was in the territory; the political framework, not military. And in order to do that, look at 2D3066, the last document. This is -- well, it says: "Negative activities and behaviour of the members of the 7th Mountain Brigade of the 3rd Corps." And it is to the president of the Presidency and the Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces, Supreme Command headquarters. And it is written on the 10th of March, 1993, which means three months prior to the events described by Mr. Siber. It is signed by the head, Fikret Muslimovic. And he was the head of the Security Department; am I right? Is that right? Of the BH Army, that is.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Fikret Muslimovic was in the Security Service of the BH Army, at the top, where the decisions are made.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Here's what he says. He says that: "The 7th Mountain Muslim Brigade, with its command in Zenica, is operating within the 3rd Corps. Several negative events and occurrences are tied to the formation of the Green Berets from this brigade, which diminishes the reputation of the BH Army and the dignity of our liberation fight, fight for freedom." It says that members of the unit, ever since their establishment, were conducting unauthorised searches of flats and houses, and that they have come into collision with the BH police and the HVO units. And then the last paragraph is the most important one, where it says: "It is obvious that the activity of members of the Green Beret units is not out of control and beyond the knowledge of the Command of the 7th Muslim Brigade, and this has given rise to serious consequences on military organisation. Opinions are widespread that behind such activities sits the leadership of the SDA in Zenica," that they are behind it, "and that this is proof that the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, only speaks of a civilian society, whereas in fact he is setting up an Islamic state." And this was written by Mr. Fikret Muslimovic in March 1993. Now, does this, Mr. Filipovic, confirm precisely what you said a moment ago in your response to Judge Antonetti's question.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I said it, perhaps I didn't. Fikret Muslimovic was one of the their strongest cadres, and in my view Delic was the number 1 man and he was the number 2 man. I had a series of verbal and other conflicts, but he noted the situation in the 3rd Corps. And later on, in 1994, Alagic complained to me and said that the 3rd Corps had received salaries or donation, whereas the 3rd Corps [as interpreted] had not, because the 3rd Corps was something different compared to the BH Army. So the 3rd Corps, Zenica, Han Bila, and so on. So that was where Alija conducted a review of troops, and so did others, Rostovo, and this was a volcano which erupted. And the result of that was that 25.000 of my fellow Travnik inhabitants couldn't remain living there, where they had lived for all their lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to correct the transcript again. On page 38, lines 19 and 20, the witness said he knew Fikret Muslimovic and that he was one of the strongest cadres, and then he went on to say that in his opinion, Rasim Delic - the name has been left out - was the number 1 man, and that the number 2 man was Fikret Muslimovic. So there's a mistake there in the transcript which mentions Filip Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. There seems to be another mistake, because if you go to line 21: "Alagic complained to me and said that the 3rd Corps had received salaries or donations, whereas the 3rd Corps had not." Is that what you wanted to say? It seems a bit contradictory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 3rd Corps did; the 7th did not. And Alagic was the commander of the 7th Corps, so the 7th Corps did not receive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you for that correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before Ms. Nozica puts her last question, I have a question. This is a document that I am seeing for the first time. I didn't know it. It's extraordinary. It's on March 10, 1993. Number 2, after Delic, seems to be challenging the 7th Mountain Brigade and is directly challenging Mr. Izetbegovic, the president of the Presidency, and he's actually sending this document to Mr. Izetbegovic. And in this document, he is accusing Mr. Izetbegovic of actually wanting to set up an Islamic state, which is contrary to the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is a political document, more than anything. Are you surprised at this? Are you surprised that a person that you knew, but he was on the other side, would actually directly challenge Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Perhaps it was wrongly interpreted or translated. But here it states clearly that the situation that he refers to in the 3rd Corps is contributing to what otherwise, in the enemy circles, is -- that they're saying that -- or, rather, the other party says that Izetbegovic is forming an Islamic state, that the 3rd Corps -- or, rather, the forces who are claiming that Alija Izetbegovic is forming an Islamic state, that everything they're doing goes to support that. So what is happening in the 3rd Corps will accelerate the situation and really help to bring it about, if they continue in that vein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I understand what you're saying. But in the BH Army, there is a chain of command. It would be Izetbegovic-Merdan-7th Brigade. Then would your answer still be valid, if this was the line of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The chain of command goes like this: Alija Izetbegovic-Delic-Mahmuljin, commander of the 3rd Corps -- so Izetbegovic-Delic -- no, no. Ah, we're dealing with March. Sefer. Alija-Sefer-Mahmuljin, who was the 3rd Corps commander, or at least I think he was at that time, or was it Hadzihasanovic, and Merdan was one of the assistants in -- he was an operations man in the 3rd Corps, but he was in the field all the time. He was in the negotiating commission and maybe also in the Joint Command, but in actual fact he co-ordinated the work of the 7th Muslim El Mujahid Unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now I have come to my last question, but -- or, rather, I was to have come to my last question, but given the witness's response, I'd like to follow on from that and say that the document does not speak about the 3rd Corps, but it says there is widespread opinion -- and that's a political assessment, according to Judge Antonetti, opinions are widespread that behind this activity there's the leadership of the SDA standing behind it in Zenica, and that this is proof that the president of the Presidency, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, is only speaking about a civilian society, whereas he's forming an Islamic state. Now, where you were in 1993, did you have this same opinion, that officially he is advocating and paying lip service to a civilian state, where in fact he is creating an Islamic state -- or secular state and he is creating an Islamic state?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, there's mention here about the Green Berets. I was asked yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I won't go back to that, but what I asked was: At the time, 1993, including this particular period and later on, did the Croats also feel that Mr. Izetbegovic was, in fact, setting up an Islamic state, whereas in his speeches he is referring to a secular state?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Might the witness be allowed to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour. Which Croats? This witness is now speaking for all Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina? I don't think he has the competence to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked about Croats in the area in which the witness was, in Central Bosnia, so I just repeated my question because the witness's answer had not been recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, please reformulate your question. Witness, have you understood the question or do you want it to be rephrased?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did answer, but I heard that it wasn't recorded. So I'll repeat what I said. All the Croats in Central Bosnia led -- with me at the head or with me at the end, considered that Alija was creating an Islamic, green Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas he keeps speaking about a civilian, secular, multi-ethnic, whatnot state. Now, what kind of state is it in which -- well, we already had the events in Busovaca and everything else that we talked about. Now, a secular, multi-ethnic state, I've already answered that, and I answered it last time too.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Filipovic. Thank you, Your Honours. I have concluded my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's time for a 20-minute break, and then the Praljak Defence will finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Praljak Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. General Praljak's Defence requests permission to allow General Praljak to start the cross-examination to deal with questions of an exclusively military nature and relating to General Praljak's meeting with the witness. But before we start the cross-examination, I would like to add that -- or, rather, tell you the link between the cross-examination of General Praljak and myself, what it has to do with the examination-in-chief and the indictment. The cross-examination will refer to paragraphs 33, 34, 37, last sentence, and paragraph 39(A) of the indictment. Now, as for the link with the examination-in-chief, we have document P1988, which was recorded on page 21 of the transcript of the 30th of November this year, followed by page 47418, line 10, also relating to the witness's testimony over the past two days, and page 47462 onwards of the same transcript, followed by page 47468 to 47470 of the 30th of November this year, and once again document P1988. Now, with the Trial Chamber's permission, General Praljak would like to start off the cross-examination with some military matters, and then I'll continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General Filipovic. I'm going to do my best to make my questions clear, as precise as a Swiss watch. So just say, Yes, No, or you don't know; affirmative, negative, or you don't know about what I'm going to ask you. Here's the first matter: You said that in May 1992, in Travnik, 50 buses arrived with roughly one and a half thousand Muslim soldiers. Now, my question is this: From which country had they come to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came from Croatia. They couldn't have come from any other country.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know, the buses that they came in, did they mostly have Croatian license plates or BH license plates?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exclusively Croatian license plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know which the last town they rallied in before they went to BH was?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know which route they took towards Travnik? Where did they pass by?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that. They could have come in from Prozor, Makljen, Gornji Vakuf, Novi Travnik, Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Across Mount Vran, following the salvation road; right?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Tomislavgrad road of salvation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, would you please wait for the general to finish his answer [as interpreted] before you -- to finish his question before you answer, and not to overlap. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: The people up there, were they wearing military uniforms when they arrived and did they have weapons?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had both uniforms and weapons, and were already a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can we, therefore, conclude that they received weapons in Croatia, and uniforms, too, and became a unit when there was an embargo enforced by the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now my question: Do you know whether anybody from Sarajevo, the government, the ministers, or whatever, gave any money to procure the weapons, uniforms, buses, the dredges along the road of salvation, or did you, yourself, ever, as a soldier of the HVO or anybody else, any remuneration or any material resources, weapons and so on, from what we call the government in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government in Sarajevo had nothing to do with this subject, the arrival of the units in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you, as the HVO of Central Bosnia, at any time receive any salaries from the central government, or weapons, shoes, uniforms; anything?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yesterday, we saw a document on the type of weapons in possession of the Army of BiH. My question would be this: In Bosnia-Herzegovina, was there, under the control of the BH Army or the HVO, any factory which manufactured rifles, automatic rifles, light machine-guns, anti-aircraft guns, cannons with one, two, or three barrels, or four barrels, Bofors weapons, ZIS multi-barrelled rocket-launchers, cannon or howitzers, 105, 122, 150-millimetre howitzers, Zolja missiles, malutka missiles, Osa missiles, RPGs or shoulder-propelled rocket-launchers, anything like that? Could any of this be produced in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing except in the Bratstvo factory which I referred to yesterday. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, none of those could have been produced in Bosnia-Herzegovina, except for the large-calibre artillery pieces at the Bratstvo factory in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: But if it's -- was it possible to find some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Pinter has kindly invited you to wait until a question is interpreted, including allowing some time for translation also. You have been overlapping totally. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when I said Bratstvo and large-calibre artillery, I meant those that had been manufactured previously. But in 1992 or 1993, it wasn't possible. I don't know about 1994, however. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, the stock of finished products at Bratstvo, how was this divvied up between the HVO and the BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I explained this already. Well, the basic thing was this: We had to agree on a single opinion, in view of the distribution of those numerous pieces there and in terms of political and military actors on both sides, such as Genjac, Tamburic, and some other individuals. So one-third went to the southern front-line, as per agreement, because down there Muslims and Croats fought together, hand by hand. One-third went to the Army of BiH, to Visoko, to their central depot. And one-third was left to me in the area where I was accepted as commander, to be shared with the Muslims, and this is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So the last third you divvied up between the Army of BiH and the HVO in the area where you were responsible; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question is as follows: If we were to -- if that -- weapons that you saw in the possession of BH Army could have been taken from the Chetniks, could have been there from previous times, or could have arrived from Croatia? Out of those three possibilities, what would be the correct answer, A, B, or C?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, each of them, in part, but 90 per cent is the answer C or the latter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So 90 per cent of the weapons came from Croatia; is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did the Army of BiH have communications such as packet radio service or satellite telephones?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did those complicated, sophisticated electronic equipment -- was it manufactured in Bosnia or was it procured through Croatia?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't manufactured in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It came from the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Fine. General Filipovic, sir, 1993, Jajce fell -- or 1992, Jajce fell. Did you immediately -- after the fall of Jajce, did you see me in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me the following, please: The Travnik HVO, where did it end up? Did it stay in the area of Travnik and Bugojno? And the Jajce HVO, the HVO forces from Jajce, after being defeated, did they stay in Travnik or did they go towards Croatia?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since up to that point Jajce saw fierce battles and manned 100 kilometres of front, and there were 4.000 fighters, half of them HVO, half of them BiH Army or the Territorial Defence, those 4.000 fighters came to the area of Travnik. And with respect to the HVO, although we tried to stop them there, make them stay there, they went and took the salvation road to Croatia, and those Muslim fighters from Jajce stayed in the area of Travnik, and some of them in the area of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did the same thing happen with the Croatian and Muslim civilians, the population? So is it true that civilians, Croats from Jajce, went to Croatia, and Muslim civilians left in the area of Travnik, Bugojno, Zenica, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fighters would not have left had the civilians stayed. Fighters left because of the civilians leaving, and the Muslim civilians stayed in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
