utterances.text: You just discussed this. It disrupted the ethnic balance and gave rise to a host of problems, that fact. So is it true that the refugees who were driven out of Central Bosnia by the Serbs, additionally complicated and brought this problem to a head?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem of refugees arriving from other areas was already present there. But when the Jajce Muslims came to the area, and we're talking about more than 20.000 people from the whole municipality of Jajce, was the final blow to the relations among the peoples in the Lasva River Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So we are faced with a thesis of the Prosecution to the effect that Praljak came up there so that we could occupy that area, drive out the Muslims, and annex the whole area to Croatia. My question to you is this: Logically speaking, how could it be possible for us to leave a whole armed brigade to enter the area, leave our people and fighters and civilians, to leave and let the alleged opponent to stay, all in order for us to attack the Muslims and drive them away? Isn't it logical, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fall of Jajce did not mean just the fall of the Jajce municipality, but also part of the Travnik municipality, and another 10.000 people, and in an area which was exclusively defended by the TO or the Army of BiH. And the front-lines of the HVO were held firm, and they repelled further advances from the Serbs. And when you came to that area, you helped the Muslims more than the Croats, because the Croats had held firm, although you did help us as well, because personally you visited two prominent elevations with me where you could see that the HVO was holding firm in the defence of the area of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Filipovic, could you please tell Their Honours whether I managed to assist more the Army of BiH and create co-operation up there - that's under A; under B, was Travnik shelled by the Serbs, and to what extent? Please relate that situation to Their Honours, what we did and what I did in that area, briefly. Did we manage to save Travnik, for instance?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Territorial Defence or the Army of BiH in Travnik was on the brink of complete disarray because exactly happened what I just explained. One-third of the territory of Travnik municipality was cleansed of its population, and particularly the inability of Hamandjici [phoen], Softici and other units who were holding the front-line there. There was panic in that area. The HVO was not cool-headed about that, because the situation was very grave. Two days after the fall of Jajce, Alija Izetbegovic stated that the HVO was to blame for the fall of Jajce, which was blasphemous, as some other of his statements. I personally took it the hardest throughout the war, the fact that Jajce fell, because I've invested quite a lot of time and my life force, and I was wounded, and my investment was in the defence of the Jajce area. And the fall of Jajce brought into question the defence of Travnik, which until that point had not been jeopardised.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, I was a volunteer, a high officer in the Croatian Army, assistant minister of defence. Which high officer of the BiH Army walked with me on the hilltops, forced people to dig trenches, organised the defence? Who, among the ranks of the BiH Army, was there with me?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody, nobody, not a single person.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And where were Valenta's [as interpreted] three battalions, and why didn't they attack Komer [phoen] and extend the corridor towards Jajce? Who was Lendo? Did he have three reserve battalions, and why didn't he attack Komer earlier on, thereby expanding the corridor towards Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction to the transcript. Line nine, it says "Valenta's three battalions." It's "Lendo's three battalions," just to avoid any misunderstanding later on. So could that be corrected. "Lendo" is the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said that there was disorganisation in Travnik and Novi Travnik, so Novi Travnik wasn't supposed to have any consequences from the fall of Jajce. And the battalions that you're referring to, they should have been active. Now, why they weren't active, I can't say at this point in time. But they had such a favourable position because we held Mravinjac, which is three to four kilometres as the crow flies, and Komer is a strategic bend from the Lasva River Valley to Vrabac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you happen to know where Lendo's family was when this fighting was going on?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that the Lendos are a large family in Opara. Now, where his family was, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, while we were organising all this, how many shells did the Serb Army use against Travnik on a daily basis? How many shells were falling on Travnik from the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska had positions around Travnik, and long-range artillery and medium-range artillery was deployed, and there were about a hundred heavy artillery shells falling on the town every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. That's what I wanted to learn from you about Travnik. Did we pull out the wounded, all the wounded, did we take care of them, and afterwards did I remain in the area? And to the best of your knowledge, how energetic was I in working towards a rapprochement between the HVO and BH Army?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't follow all your activities, there were so many of them, but I do know that you had an overall influence, or your arrival did, with respect to the defence of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was it negative or positive?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there can be any dilemmas on that score. It was all positive, your positive involvement in matters of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now look at document 4D01611, please. Yesterday, there was a question as to where Izetbegovic's signature was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, the number is 4D01611, if I may correct you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: On the 14th of June, Mr. Filipovic, had Travnik already fallen? June 1993.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Kiseljak, on the 10th, I crossed over, and on the 11th, I was engaged in heavy fighting to stabilise the line and to prevent the opposite side from breaking through deeper.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me, at the end of March and beginning of April 1993, did you see me again in the town of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was surprised to see you moving around quite normally in Travnik, without any escorts or anything like that. I came across you, and you were sitting in front of a cafe where nobody usually sat, and you were sitting there alone. That's not the kind of thing we did over there, any of our commanders over there or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's correct. I remember that, too, Mr. Filipovic. But in Travnik, what was the ratio of HVO soldiers compared to the BH Army of the 17th, 7th, or whatever unit? What was the ratio, the proportion of the two sides' soldiers in Travnik in 1993, April?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a ratio of 5:1, roughly, to the advantage of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And what about the ratio of the population, Croats, Bosniak Muslims; what was that ratio at the time?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the 1991 population census, there was a negligible amount of Muslims, whereas at that time already the ratio was 3:1 in favour of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now look at the document. Doesn't it say here that this document was delivered to -- or, rather, delivery of the text of the order issued in Geneva -- now, if it arrived by packet link, could there have been any signatures? Because when you have a packet link communication, there is no signature, right, just like the other ones that Blaskic sent and so on earlier on?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There cannot be a signature, in technical terms. It's technically not feasible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, point 4, it says: "The Presidency --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Witness, you said it's technically not possible to have a signature. This document has -- oh, I'm sorry, I'm looking at the wrong one. I apologise. No, actually, I was looking at the right one, 4D01611. You have a letterhead of the "Hrvatska Zajednica Herceg-Bosna," and you have, on the left side, an entry that is handwritten. Now, can you explain to me how it comes that it is possible to write figures by hand, but not possible to sign by hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This reaches us via the Main Staff of the HVO in order for us to receive it quicker. I see nothing strange there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Maybe I did not express myself correctly. You were asked how was this document, of which we have a photocopy before us, how was that transmitted, and it was suggested that it was transmitted by packet. And then you were asked, Is it possible to transmit by packet a document with a signature? And you say, No, that is not possible. Now, I assume that everything else is accurate. Then I am amazed to find that this document has figures -- the registration figures put on top left by hand, and I do not understand why it would then not be possible also to have a signature put there by hand. And that's what I would like you to explain to me. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This is a question to the witness, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these technical matters, you want a clear, precise answer. Now, if you consider that Alija Izetbegovic did not send this document, or, rather, write it, that's one thing. And the way in which it was sent to us, well, that's what I'm talking about. I don't know what the technology of sending a document like this was. There was some packet link, documents were delivered in one way or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, you did not say that when you were asked. You gave a clear answer, although you did not know. Is that not the case? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The order is that there be immediate cessation of all hostilities between the units, et cetera, et cetera. To me, this is logical that it was written and that it arrived. I don't know what it was that I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We're not talking about what is written in the document. We're talking about the fact that first you have, without "if"s or "when"s, confirmed this was sent by package to you, and it is not possible to send such a document by package to you with a signature. But there are other handwritten notes, so maybe this was not sent by package to you. I regard this as probable, or there is -- but I find no explanation. It does not go together, what you said. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. I apologise. One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, please read out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I am asking the witness now, and I have not received an answer. So if you want to go on, then go on, but I stop at this and I find that I did not get a satisfactory answer. You can go on now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: If that was what was wanted -- now, it says "delivery of the text of the orders." That means that somebody from Geneva received instructions, not an order. Petkovic would have written an order; is that right? The BH Army, they write "Naredba"?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's start from the beginning, let's go back to the beginning. Somebody in Geneva --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I follow my fellow Judge's question that remains unanswered, and I'm also quite disturbed by it. There are three, if not four, possibilities; at least three. The first possibility: This is a forgery, this document. It has been manufactured for the case. After the conflict, it was archived in the Croatian National Archives to convey the impression that Mr. Izetbegovic was working hand in hand with the HVO. That's the first possibility. Second possibility: There is a packet switch communication, so the information is sent by packet, but the sender does not include the figures "02-2/," et cetera. He does not mention it because he is in a hurry and he forgot about it. So it is sent, the document is sent, because you know, when you send by packet there can be no handwritten mention at all. And then later on, at a later stage, the officer, or the soldier sending the document, noted that he had forgotten to register the document. So in his own hand, he wrote "02-2/1-01-1058/93." And then when the conflict ended, all the archives were collected, and this very document was archived in the National Archives. So that's the second possibility. That could be an explanation, in my book, because as was said by Judge Trechsel, you cannot have a document that is sent by packet with anything handwritten in it, because that could mean that you could also sign the document. And anyone with a bit of knowledge about it knows that it is then done electronically, and it is sent off straight away. But Judge Trechsel wants to add something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Having re-examined this, my conclusion and hypothesis is the following one: There are two steps in this communication. The first goes from Geneva to the General Staff, and that's a packet communication. There, this document is received, and then it is copied on this paper with the letterhead, and the signature is put in by hand. And in this revised form, it is then distributed. Could that be the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's like this: I'll take it in detail, looking at the document. The Main Staff of the HVO -- "delivery of the text of the order issued by the Presidency of the RBiH in Geneva on," et cetera, and this text -- this order is delivered to all the operations zones; not only the Central Bosnia zone, but all the operations zones. Now, it could have been sent by normal post, except to us in the operative zone in Vitez of Central Bosnia, because at that point in time all communications had been cut off. So it could have reached us a month later, when a helicopter landed. Every seven days or once a fortnight, that's when the post was brought in. That's why I said as far as the technology goes -- well, we've lost a lot of time over this. I see no need to spend so much time. But this case has been going on for a very long time, so I suppose you can afford the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The responsibility for the time is with us, not with you, Witness. You don't have to worry about it. It's none of your concern. Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's see how the army functioned. I send an order to Tihomir Blaskic, for example. What does Blaskic do in that case? Does he take the order, transcribe it, put his reference number, and issue orders further down the line, or does he just send out my order? What is customary in the army? How does the army go about this?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blaskic has to send his order to his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So Alija Izetbegovic sends this man over here an order. What does he do? To Petkovic here. I'm pointing to him, this man here [indicates]. What does he do then?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In line with what I've said, he writes out his own order for his own purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Does he put a reference number of his own?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So the Main Staff -- the chief of the Main Staff issues an order to his units which he has received from the president of the Presidency, so he conveys the original order, not "zapovjed," as command; is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could not have been otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In that case, Witness, would not General Petkovic sign as Chief of Staff, rather than send a paper which says: "Signed, president" -- or not signed -- yes, it says: "Signed: President of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic," if it is now Petkovic's order? Actually, we have seen a number of these kind of orders which have been handed on. First they came from Mate Boban, and then the next they went -- from the General Staff, they went to the operation zones, and there the chief of the General Staff handed this on as his order, as you have correctly stated. I fully agree with the way you have stated this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, you see in item 2 it says: "Persons responsible for fulfillment of this order are: Commander of the Army of the BiH, Rasim Delic, and Commander of HVO General Staff, Milivoj Petkovic." So he conveyed that to impress upon us from which level this comes or to impart the significance of that. He did not introduce - I mean Petkovic - not a single element of his wording or phraseology. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Only the reference number?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I meant he did not introduce anything of his into the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is this document, as you see it, registered in the Main Staff under a reference number?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: This command, does it refer in item 2 to the commander of the Army of BiH, Rasim Delic, and commander of HVO General Staff, Milivoj Petkovic? You see "Komandant" and "Zapovjednik." There's a difference between the two components. The first the Muslim uses JNA terminology and the HVO uses Croatian terminology; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Okay. How much time do we have left?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please take a look at document 1D03151.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I would like to know the answer to your question. How much time do you have left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have used 25 minutes already. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, so the document is 1D03151. Is this document something which was called a regulation in the JNA, or a law, entitled "Brigade Rules," how brigades should be run, et cetera; is that correct, Mr. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brigade Rules was equivalent to a Bible in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. So page 201, "Structure of the defence zone of a brigade," you must know them by heart, don't you?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, it was the Bible in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please answer my question. Did you know everything in that Bible?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Here, what is discussed is what should one be mindful, if he's a brigade commander, with respect to the rear. So my question is whether he is mindful only of military matters or also of civilian matters.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade commander is exclusively responsible for military matters, but he does co-ordinate matters, civilian matters, which have ramifications on his defence efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: It discusses a proper brigade, full complement of soldiers, et cetera. Could you please tell Their Honours, how many tanks are there in an armoured brigade, usually?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Battalion, 40; battalion, 43; battalions -- 120, just tanks, not counting other armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Those tanks require ammunition, fuel, workshop for repairs, and it must be secured in the rear, if not close to the front-lines?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, there are logistics bases in the rear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Then you have to provide dormitories, trucks, and that area is safeguarded by the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm not going through this book, what is written in it. Please tell me the following: What has this model brigade in common with what you had as a brigade in the HVO at that time? What did your HVO brigade -- what did it have, in terms of all the facilities?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would illustrate this with a frozen sea. The top layer of ice is the front-line, and there is no ice deeper where the water is fluid. This would be equivalent to people who manned the front-lines and sleep at their homes, until 1994, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: You mean that we do not have any in-depth area, we barely hold on to the front-line?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to two kilometres is under our control from the very front-line. We do not have any rear, in terms of deep territory for a brigade to defend itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Were there areas where this width was smaller than two kilometres?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Please adhere to the rules and wait for each other. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would just add: We gave a few extra minutes to Ms. Alaburic, and the same will apply to you. So if you are a few minutes above today and under these special circumstances, we will not be as strict as we have been at other times. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So up to two kilometres, was this the maximum width? But most frequently, what was the width, depending on the lay of the land?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the trenches, it was two kilometres. But as a tactician, I could say that it was up to two kilometres, but in essence it was five metres at places. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Filipovic, for coming here, for providing me with answers. I apologise once again for the overlap. It's something that really happens because we are quite lively when we discuss those matters. I apologise to Their Honours, to the interpreters, and everyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have three follow-up questions for you, Witness, because we're going to turn into JNA specialists with the text we have in front of us. Indeed, we really go into detail, but details are important. As I understand it, based on the JNA texts, and since there were JNA officers in the HVO, BH Army, and the VRS, everybody must have worked the same way, and you were a lieutenant-colonel in the JNA, therefore a higher-ranking officer, a senior officer very knowledgeable in military matters; hence, the relevant questions and questions of interest put to you. So according to the JNA, a defence zone must be, at most, 20 kilometres, but as this document says, this is the brigade that is holding this in-depth positioning that is 20 kilometres. And the document says, regarding the defence of the battalion, it is only two to three kilometres' long. And then General Praljak asked you questions about the number of tanks in the brigade, and you said that the HVO brigades, as a matter of fact, did not have the necessary means, and the defence zone was not 20 kilometres, but it was, at most, 2 kilometres. Is this really what you are telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is breadth along the front-line. In this case, as I've already explained, the brigade in Jajce had to man 100 kilometres of defence line, but in our case, on average, each brigade defended 10 kilometres, the length of the front-line would be 10 kilometres. But depth of the zone was two kilometres, up to two kilometres, from the very front-line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been very accurate. We'll all keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one correction. In line 18, what is reflected in the transcript is that the witness said "but the zone was two kilometres." The witness did not say the zone was two kilometres, but the depth was two kilometres, up to two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Coric. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like you to permit me to ask one military question to the major general, given the discussion that we've had. Do you allow me? Very briefly, one military question. General, since we are discussing a combat activity zone, allow me to say that I do know the HVO-controlled territory in Central Bosnia quite well. Would you agree with me that the overall area in Central Bosnia, particularly you said that there were distances of 800 metres between front-lines, that whole area was a combat activity zone? Would you agree with me if I said so? And if it was not, could you please tell us, what was the area in Central Bosnia which was not part of a combat activity zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the broader sense of the word, the whole area was a combat activity zone. I would say that it's up to the range of the enemy's artillery or weapons. There were areas which were not in the combat activity area or zone, or had no contact with the enemy because they were in too deep, but I could agree that this would expend more than two kilometres from the front-line when it comes to the combat activity zone. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] I agree with you. What was the point in Central Bosnia that BH Army artillery could not reach?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they can reach all points with their rifles, let alone artillery. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for your answer. I hope it's in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a second question regarding Jajce. I listened to you very carefully. We understand that the BH Army and the HVO withdrew towards Travnik. You mentioned the high number of soldiers that were present, and you told us that the HVO soldiers had left and left the Muslims on the ground, and you said that for you it was a crucial factor; this fact that the Muslims stayed on in Travnik, that changed the situation. And when I heard you say that, I wondered what would have happened if the HVO had stayed. Would things have changed in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had the Croats stayed at Travnik after the fall of Jajce, they would have restored the order between the two communities in Travnik before Jajce fell, but Croatians could not stay in Travnik because by that time half a million or a million Muslims fled to Croatia as refugees. They knew what their life would be in Travnik and what their living conditions would be in Croatia or in a third country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question. I was very surprised by a question put to you by General Praljak. You said that every day at least 100 shells would fall on Travnik. I went to Travnik, and I did not have the impression that Travnik had been as destroyed as Vukovar or Stari Grad, say. So if there are shells falling on a town, they destroy houses, are you really sure that there were a hundred shells falling daily, destroying houses, because I didn't see the damage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You destroy a town if you kick things about. In absolute terms, 100 artillery shells is not too much, it's not a large number. Of course, it affects civilians and those on the receiving end. I don't know whether you noticed impact sites on buildings or the repairs made to those places, but what I said was maybe only a fraction of what really hit the town. And I refer to the period when Mr. Praljak was in town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying part of the town what hit and there were impacts on the walls. It's true. When you go to Travnik, you see all these impacts, but the houses weren't razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not necessarily they are razed to the ground. I, myself, saw 100 shells, heavy shells, hit the Borac factory within one and a half hours, for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, that's very clear. Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just another question with regard to this artillery fire and shelling. There are, of course, quite different ways of shelling. There are grenades that explode when they hit the ground, and they will cause destructions, and there are those that explode in the air, before touching ground, with splinters all around dangerous for any soft target. Now, were you saying that the hundred shells were all impact shells, or was a proportion of them shells that exploded before hitting actually a building or a street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the JNA we used to fiddle with those fuses, time-operated fuses, but such -- their ratio was 15 to 20 per cent with respect to those impact shells that were a majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter, just before the break. I believe you can finish before the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best to finish by the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have before you the documents where it says "3D --" documents marked "3D." Now, as we have little time, we're going to skip over some of them, but I'd like to discuss 3D01731 with you now. First of all, let me ask you whether you know Davor Kolenda.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can you recognise his -- would you be able to recognise his signature and whether it's on the end of that document? Do you know him that well or not?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Davor Kolenda is a nephew of mine, and I know exactly what that looks like.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So you can confirm that that is his signature, can you?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The next thing I want to ask you is this: I'd like to go through the statement, and Davor Kolenda was in Travnik in 1992 and 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with his whole family, his parents, and my parents too.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did he have a position of any kind?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the last month or two, he was one of the clerks in the civilian government, the Municipal Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, in this statement he says that he was arrested. Do you know anything about that, that he was arrested sometime around the 20th of April, 1993, by the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, moving from Manjac [phoen] to Kalibunar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Does the name Ivo Fistic ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivo Fistic was also a clerk. He was one of his colleagues. He was taken to Orasac or Han Bila and was incarcerated there for days and months.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: We're talking about 1993 now, are we, all the time?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, do you know whether Davor Kolenda conducted negotiations with the Serbs about pulling out civilians, Croats?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A few days before the people left to go up there, he went to Vlasic and had a meeting with Slobodan, who was his best man or a kum, and the Serbs respected the fact that the people had passed through the territory of Republika Srpska, but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat what he said at the end?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What people are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My people, my people from Travnik, except for my parents, who remained in Travnik. So throughout the fighting of the last 10 months, my parents were in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: In 1993. And what about the people that went across Mount Vlasic; were they Croats? Are you referring to Croats?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Why were they leaving?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We'd been talking about the pressures, the sporadic shooting, flags, banners, clothing, conduct, arrests, people being released, and on the map I pointed out four points at which communications were severed, but communications were cut off at many more places. So there was general uncertainty and firing. Do you know what it's like when there are bullets whizzing past your head all the time? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It means that there was fighting, combat.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fighting, combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, did you know about an order from Colonel Blaskic about moving the soldiers from Novi Bila, from [indiscernible] on page 5?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's also page 5 of the English text. I have to repeat that. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did you know about Blaskic's order on pulling out to Nova Bila, both the soldiers and the people?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who replaced me as commander of the brigade, Leutar, once the people had gathered together by the church in Ovcarevo which is just two hours away from the Serbs, he tried to dissuade them, whereas he arrived in an UNPROFOR vehicle, and he saw what the situation was like. And when he did, he went back to the command, to headquarters, and reported back about the situation. I assumed that Blaskic then issued his order whereby the units -- well, if the people couldn't be prevented from leaving, then the Travnik Brigade should be transferred across Mount Vlasic and the area that was still not controlled by the BH Army - at least he thought so - and should be moved to the lower part of Travnik municipality and Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The people who were gathering there in front of the church in Ovcarevo, did anybody persuade them to leave the Travnik area and go to Herzegovina [realtime transcript read in error "Sarajevo"]?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a senseless question. I have to say no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I have to ask you that.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: One more question. Do you know that Kolenda was in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kolenda was in Manjaca with 800 or 900 people for some 15 days, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: How did he come to be there?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all the military-able men were transported by the Serbs from there to Manjaca, and Manjaca was already at that time, and later on, a synonym for suffering and the impossibility of being a human being -- allowed to be a human being in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There is a problem in transcript, in order to -- in order to avoid any possible mistakes later. It is line 12 on the current page, 71. My dear colleague asked whether anybody was trying to persuade the people to go to Herzegovina. The transcript said "to Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I couldn't have asked about Sarajevo. The indictment says "Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: According to the statement that we're discussing now, and on the basis of the questions I've been asking you - I'm saying this for the record, that we're going through the statement - that 454 soldiers and 50 policemen, a total of 504 soldiers, then left for Manjaca and that they were military conscripts aged between 15 and 55 years. Did Davor Kolenda tell you anything about that, about the age of the people who were taken to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said, the military-able men from 18 years old to -- I'm not sure about 55. Maybe even 60.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What about 15-year-olds?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, depending on the age group. If somebody had documents to prove when they were born, then -- well, then these were minors. But the Serbs didn't make a selection of any kind, whether 15 years old or 18 years old. If they were able-bodied, they were taken away.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on page 9 of this document, this is what it says: "On the 18th of June, 1993, in co-operation with the local priest in Borovice, held a meeting with the locals and asked them not to flee their homes. We promised them that we would defend them, and in Vares there were already a lot of refugees from Vares and Kraljeva Sutjeska." Do you have any knowledge about that, about what it says here? First of all, do you know where Borovice is?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Borovice is an important village in Vares municipality. They passed through Vares municipality and were deployed in the defence over there. However, at that time the intensity of the fighting and attacks by the BH Army were such that -- well, because of Kakanj and the Kakanj refugees, they were not able to do that, especially --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: We've dealt with that document. Now I need less than one minute. Just take a look at 3D03792, please. And it's a document which is directly linked to P1988. It follows on from that document, when we spoke about the Joint Command. It's a document written by -- it says here "Colonel Filip Filipovic." Is that you? Did you write this document, and do you know anything about the document?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The document dated the 21st of June, 1993. It's about a joint command, and international factors included, who ask for a resolute answer, a clear response from you.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a member of the Joint Command, and probably as a result of the meeting with the representatives of the international community, this was written as an inquiry, as a query, what to do. Let me repeat. It was once again the period of intensive fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it's my document. I see the way it's written and this FF; written by FF and typed out by KB. I'm trying to remember who the KB was. Other people didn't do it in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: But I'm asking you, because it says "Colonel Filip Filipovic." Is that you?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So does it follow from this that you were a member of the Joint Command already at that time, that is to say, on the 21st of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, nobody abolished it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Had Travnik already fallen at that time?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I've completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we'll break in a few minutes, but I have a question, a question that I already wanted to put to you yesterday. Now that we have some time, I'll put it to you now. Yesterday, we saw a video where there was the meeting between Petkovic, Halilovic, and so on, and others, and you were there. And we also saw that there was a Spaniard chairing the meeting. I was thinking about it overnight, and I wondered the following: This was a meeting where you were face to face, you know, the HVO was in front of the BH Army. I would like to know whether you had your weapons with you or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there were any weapons, it was of the order of a pistol. But I personally didn't have a weapon, and I don't know that anybody did, although the people that were escorts at the back, the BH Army, they probably did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a tent. Could you tell us whether it was the Spaniards who put up the tent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the provisional base of the Spanish Battalion, so, yes, it was their tent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: An observation to the transcript. Page 74, line 3, the "21" before "June" got lost. It was said, "21st of June."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will break for 20 minutes, and then Mr. Scott will start his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. You may proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good evening to Your Honours, all those in and around the courtroom. Good evening, Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I want to start at least this evening in a fairly chronological way. You left the JNA with a rank of colonel on 10 April 1992; yes?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-colonel, but I was supposed to be promoted to the rank of colonel that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And at that particular time, sir, why did you leave the JNA?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the JNA was no longer JNA. It was something completely different. I'll give you an example. A person with whom I spent 20 years of service, who used to be a Yugoslav and he followed the Yugoslav line fraternity, brotherhood, unity of all the people, well, that person, I found out one day that he just moved to the Republika Srpska Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not sure that helps us a great deal. Can you tell us, without telling me a story? Can you just give your reasons why you left the JNA in mid-April 1992?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have left it in 1991, when I saw the columns leaving Vukovar, hundreds of people under arms who were singing, "We will slaughter the Croats, send us some salad to go with it." And since I was high in command circles, I knew which units were engaged in attacking Vukovar. And when you see on TV that a line of Chetniks appears, I knew that it wouldn't have been possible without the knowledge of the highest ranks, and I would have left then and there. But my wife was seriously ill, she contracted cancer and she waited for surgery, so I waited until April of 1992 to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, some of these things will seem obvious to you, but we have to make a record in this courtroom and make sure that we have things as clear as possible. When you say, I saw the columns leaving Vukovar, in your view, what military force had attacked Vukovar and was causing these problems that you've briefly indicated?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that the JNA had, the best units that they had according to the standards of the time, the 1st Guards Division, the Novi Sad Armoured Corps, and I knew that from Backa Palanka an artillery brigade. So the strongest units that the JNA had were sent to Vukovar, and the best personnel was JNA, but then you see a line of Chetniks and you realise that this is no longer a JNA, Yugoslav People's Army. And this was when I realised that it was something completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you say it was something different, can I understand you to say it had become a -- did you consider it a Serb army? Is that what you're suggesting, in so many words?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, did you consider the JNA, as of least April 1992, if not sooner, but did you consider the JNA, as of April 1992, to be the enemy of the Croat people or at least Croatia?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, enemy to the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then you arrived in the Lasva Valley on the 12th of April, 1992, and for a few weeks you were considered yourself to be the number 1 officer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Scott. Given the questions put by the Prosecutor, I must mention for the record that as far as I'm concerned, I could not ask questions on these parts because I'm also seized of a case, of the Vukovar case in another trial, so I cannot ask questions. I wanted that to be on record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you arrived in the Lasva Valley. You became for a time the senior Croat commander on the ground, if I can put it that way. You either knew or became aware that Mr. Petkovic left the JNA and had joined the HV and then came to Bosnia-Herzegovina around the same time?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when he came. I know when I came.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look, please, at P00163. It should be in the binder. I'm not sure if the witness -- thank you very much, Usher. P00163. Sir, this is an order over the name of Janko Bobetko, dated the 16th of April, 1992, very close to the time you arrived -- you say you arrived in the Lasva Valley, appointing 11 individuals to the command of the Grude Forward Command Post, including Mr. Petkovic, among others, including Mr. Bruno Stojic. And can you tell us when you first, upon arriving in the Lasva Valley, became aware that there was a command centre at Grude called a forward command post and that Mr. Petkovic was in charge of that?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be around mid-April 1992. That would be a couple of days after I'd arrived to the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you could next direct your attention to the exhibit immediately before that one, P00162. If you turn back, please, one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Scott. Your question was not answered. Witness, the question was whether you had been aware of the creation of that command post. You have told us that it's about -- when you arrived - you arrived a bit earlier, I think - but were you aware of it? Did you know there was this forward command post in Grude?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse me, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When did you first learn -- you arrive on the ground. You're trying to establish some sort of an armed force in that area. When did you learn that there was some other people trying to do something similar, perhaps at a higher level; that there were people in Grude, or Mostar, or someplace else like this? What's described here in general, when did you first find that out?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already stated, five, six, or seven days after I arrived to the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So by approximately the 18th or 19th of April, 1992, you became aware of this organisation in Grude and Mr. Petkovic's involvement there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I knew about Petkovic, but I did know that there was a command that I was supposed to link up with or establish communication with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That was part of my question, sir. So when did you? At some point, presumably, sir, given the nature of your involvement there -- you've told us you were involved at a very high level, you were the number 1 commander for a very short time, then became deputy to Mr. Blaskic a few weeks later. Surely, sir, at some time you became aware of some of the people who were at this forward command post in Grude. When did you first become aware that Mr. Petkovic was in charge or command of that forward command post?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, towards the last third of April, I went to Grude to establish contacts with that command post, and it is there that I met Mr. Petkovic, got to know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in connection with the exhibit that I asked you about a few moments ago, P00162, can you confirm it was your experience, when you arrived at Grude on this occasion you've just told us about, as reflected in paragraph number 2 of this document, you did, in fact, find that Mr. Petkovic was in charge, he was the commander?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived at Grude one day after Grude had been shelled. They relocated to the basement of the hotel. There was no electricity there. There were candles lit --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to ask your co-operation, sir, in answering my questions as succinctly as you can. I didn't ask you if anything had been shelled. My question to you was: When, in fact -- when did you, in fact, find that -- did you find, on going to Grude, that Mr. Petkovic was in charge as the commander? And the answer to that question is either, Yes, No, I don't know, and I don't need to know about whether it was shelled or not. Did you find out, when you got to Grude on that occasion, that Mr. Petkovic was the commander of the forward command post; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I spoke to several people. Among them was Petkovic in the basement with the electricity and a candle --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When did you find out he was the commander?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in May or June, by that time I learned that he was a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you learn at some point -- I'm directing your attention to paragraph number 6 of P00162. Did you learn at some point that also -- that Mr. Bruno Stojic was involved at the Grude Command Post in connection with logistical support?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to Petkovic, Roso, Bender, and Jozo Maric. Stojic was not there, or at least not at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me repeat my question. Did you learn at some point that Mr. Bruno Stojic was involved at the Grude Command Post in connection with logistical support?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you understand that Mr. Petkovic -- or come to understand that Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Stojic, among others, had been placed in these positions by General Bobetko?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no idea about Bobetko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, there were other officers who had left the JNA -- who left the JNA and joined the Croatian forces. You knew that -- was that Mr. Petkovic, himself; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Blaskic served in Slovenia and had left the JNA several months before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Siljeg came from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, Ivica Rajic, came from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivica Rajic came sometime in June 1992 from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you indicated, in response to a question from Ms. Alaburic, that in some cases you thought there was a lack of trust toward you because of your JNA background. But as you've just indicated, sir, isn't it correct that there were a substantial number of Croatian officers -- Croat officers who had come from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, an objection to the lack of precision in this question. I do not understand what "substantial number" means, given that my learned colleague listed three or four people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, let's not split hairs. Of course, the word "substantial" could be 5, 10, 100, but this is a clever witness. He's clever enough to really adjust the question as need may arise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those names were the only ones in for the general HVO personnel. What I spoke about was the Lasva River Valley, and they numbered three or four.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say "they numbered three or four," what do you mean; that there were three or four former JNA officers on the Croat side in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I can list their names, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can do it very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Lovrinovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Jazbinski, that would be it - and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Colonel Blaskic, too, correct, and Mr. Rajic?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No, that would be Kiseljak. Those two were at Kiseljak. That's not the Lasva River Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Now, let me ask you, were you or to your knowledge, any of these persons, were you or Mr. Petkovic or Mr. Siljeg or Mr. Blaskic, or Mr. Rajic, any of the other former JNA officers, were any of you accused or prosecuted for treason, or anything such as that, for leaving the JNA and joining the other side?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, I've not been.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you would agree, wouldn't you, that Muslims had at least as much right to leave the JNA and join the BiH armed forces as you and Petkovic and Blaskic had to leave the JNA?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them had the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, likewise, at a later time, for the same reason, sir, that you and others wanted to leave the JNA when you considered the JNA the enemy of the Croatian people, you would agree, sir, that the Muslims had the right to leave the HVO and join their side, if you want to put it that way, when they decided that the HVO was the enemy of their people; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, but let me tell you that the Serbs were the first to leave the JNA, many individuals from the command that I was at, not just --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You've answered my question. And in fact, sir, that's the view you expressed at the time, that you felt that if the Muslims wanted to leave the HVO and join either -- what was initially the Territorial Defence, which became the ABiH or armija, you felt that they had a right to do so? And just to confirm what you're saying today, you gave the same testimony in the Kordic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you arrived in the Lasva Valley -- and you said in your testimony on -- let me say that and put a time on this. When you gave your testimony on Monday, you described as the beginning of the war being April, May, and June of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as I understand your testimony, sir, and from the summary of your expected testimony which was provided by Mr. Petkovic's counsel, when you arrived around the 12th of April, 1992, you found things to be, shall we say, fairly disorganised, confused?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you arrived there, did you find that there was a Croat armed force ready-made, already existing, waiting for you to take command, or did you find yourself basically, essentially, at a starting point to begin to build an armed force largely from, we would say, scratch?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I encountered armed individuals, but their level of organisation was far from something that could be labelled an army. They only had the wish and the will to take part in defence or to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as things developed around April and May of 1992, in fact, the Croats and Muslims were doing many similar things at the same time to develop and organise armed forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, in fact, probably the key officers on both sides at that time, and when I say "both sides," I'm now saying the Croats and the Muslims or Bosniaks, were indeed former JNA officers; correct? There were a number of former JNA officers who had joined the Muslim armed forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, in fact, as things developed, there were actually more professional soldiers -- more JNA officers who joined the Muslim armed forces than joined the Croat forces in April, May, June 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to the Croatian forces. Nobody joined the Croatian forces or the HVO. They joined the Territorial Defence or the ABiH, when it referred to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies if I misspoke. I did mean to say that there were a larger number, in fact, of former JNA professional officers who joined the Muslim armed forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it also fair to say, sir, that by May or June of 1992, in fact, the Muslim armed forces, again whether you want to call it at that time the Territorial Defence or the ABiH, in terms of personnel or manpower, was a larger armed force than the Croat side, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in numbers they were larger.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, likewise, at that time the Muslim armed force had a larger number -- larger percentage of professional former JNA officers in its officer corps, didn't it, or didn't they?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a factor of several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you've told us now a couple of times it was approximately the 15th of May, 1992, when something like -- I heard once 1500, another time 2.000 Muslim soldiers or armed forces arrived in the Travnik area; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a unit arrived, the difference of what had gone on before, and this one was that in mid-May a unit of 1500 people arrived. They had weapons, they had commanders. A whole unit arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And you testified on Monday, sir, and I just want to confirm that I understood correctly. You said that as of June 1992, the Territorial Defence or the BH Army was at a point where it could carry its part of the burden and responsibility, it was on a footing of equality, it was able to fight and man the defence lines. Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I thought that the Prosecutor was going to stay with that topic, but he moved on. I have a big problem with the document that we've seen to start with, in which Colonel Petkovic could be standing in for Bobetko, and in which an assignment is given to Mr. Coric [as interpreted]. This is a document of the Croatian Army. There's no doubt about it. So back in April 1992, there was a document saying that there are two individuals, Petkovic and Coric [as interpreted], fulfilling specific tasks and positions in that forward command post set up in Grude. The document is dated 16th of April. Remember, yesterday I asked you a question. I wanted to know whether or at what time, in your view, General Petkovic was Chief of Staff. I didn't know then that the Prosecutor was going to present you with this document, because I'd asked myself when General Petkovic took position, took office. And you said that you met General Petkovic and you spoke about the situation, but when you met with General Petkovic, did he tell you that when Bobetko was absent, he would be the one in charge in the Croatian Army? Had he told you this, what impact would that have had on you? What would your impression have been if General Petkovic had told you, Well, look, I'm actually wearing two hats; I'm on the southern front in the Croatian Army, but at the same time I am a Chief of Staff in the HVO? Because this document raises a problem which cannot be dodged at all, so I'm trying to understand the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this document introduces Bobetko, but I did not know anything about Bobetko or the southern front. I'm discussing the first moment when I met Petkovic, when I met Roso and Bender, as I said, and I'm not at all interested in how this whole thing is structured. I did not have a standard structured command up there either. My task was to create units, create command structures. I cannot tell you precisely when I learned about whether that was a forward command post or when the Main Staff was set up and that Petkovic was at the head of that Main Staff. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can't answer. I'm not going to continue on this line, but another question. In this document, it seems that there is a need to co-ordinate combat action on the southern front. This is what we have in the heading of the document. Now, this makes me wonder, isn't this -- we have a situation where the HV is present because its territory is in jeopardy, they believe they need to have an advance command post up to Grude, but at the same time they have a, quote/unquote "agreement" with the HVO so that the HVO, hand in hand with the HV, co-operate against the common enemy, which are the Serbs, and in the framework of this co-ordination, and there could be two entities, the HV and the HVO, and of course because there's co-ordination there needs to be a chief, and a priori it's Bobetko, but whenever Bobetko is not there, it's the other man who takes over, i.e., Petkovic, does this make any sense, militarily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That area of, that is to say, Herzegovina and Croatia, is a united area, geographically speaking, but also vis-a-vis the enemy, because at that time, to the west of Mostar, some 10 kilometres to the west, and all Mostar was held by the Serbs. Not only did they hold Mostar, but they held the area to the west of Mostar. So co-ordinated action was designed to see that the aggressor, the enemy, the army that was being formed, the Army of Republika Srpska, the previous JNA, should be removed. So the answer is that without that, there couldn't have been any co-ordination between the armed forces of both areas and both countries, both states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you correctly, according to you co-ordination was possible between the HVO and the HV against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have the floor, but I believe that this document created a problem and I wanted to go into more depth. But I'm sure we'll see in depth, you know, whenever Mr. Petkovic comes to testify. I'm sure we'll see the document again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Probably so, Your Honour. Before I continue, Mr. President, just to correct the record, and I noticed there were several people in the courtroom who noticed, and if the President will allow, there were several references a few minutes ago to it being Mr. Petkovic and Coric, and I think the record should reflect it was Petkovic and Stojic. I think there won't be any dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, turning on -- moving on, now, if I could ask you to be brief because you've probably learned by now that time is a bit of a precious resource here, what do you consider the characteristics and skills of a good officer?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he be well trained, a professional so that he can do the business of an officer, honesty, loyalty. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How about information? How about situational knowledge, if you will, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I said capacitated and well trained as a professional, that would incorporate all of that kind thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And during your military career, sir, did you consider yourself a good officer?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to the time you were the commander of the Travnik Brigade, from approximately the latter part of October of 1992 until the latter part of April of 1993. Who did you report to during that time as your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And during that time, did you have a deputy commander of the Travnik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a time, it was Lovrinovic. Then it was, well, the person who was killed in Sarajevo, Leutar, Leutar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in addition to having a deputy, I don't know did at the brigade level, but did you have a Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Leutar was the deputy, then Lovrinovic was the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what did you consider the principle duties and responsibilities of your deputy? What did you expect from them as their commander?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to add something. I had a deputy who was the late Nikola Grbesa. He was killed when Jajce fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell me what kind of functions and responsibilities you expected or performance you expected from your deputy?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expected that what I was to Blaskic for a time -- that is to say, that the deputy should, in the spirit of an agreement with the commander, should perform the functions of replacing the commander at all places where the commander was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, apart from the replacement function, which certainly is an important one, but absent actually replacing the commander absence in his or her absence, what have you, what would be the other ongoing daily duties of a deputy vis-a-vis you, as the commander?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Combat, the defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you consider, at the time when they were in this position, Mr. Lovrinovic and Mr. Leutar, did you consider them to be essentially your right-hand man, if I can use that term?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, associates, right-hand man, yes, in matters that had to be accomplished.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what sorts of communication procedures or meetings existed among the command staff at that time; you, Mr. Lovrinovic, Mr. Leutar, perhaps others, just to keep the command up to date, share information? Did you have a daily meeting, morning meeting, did you have a weekly meeting? What sort of things did you have in place to keep the command staff, if you will, on the same page?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, daily morning briefings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As of approximately the 1st of April, 1993, how many soldiers were actually under your command in the Travnik Brigade, approximately?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About one and a half thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And we've heard in this case about -- that military members, HVO, and other -- and TO, other forces, did a lot of their military service by what's been described as shifts? Was that true in the Travnik Brigade; were people essentially deployed or assigned on shifts?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And at any given time, assuming you weren't actually in a combat situation and active fighting going on, assuming you don't have active fighting, approximately how many HVO soldiers in the Travnik area would be on the line or on a shift at any given time?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And perhaps the answer is the number you gave me a moment ago, but just to be clear: If, indeed, active fighting started, how many HVO soldiers could the Travnik Brigade, around April 1993 -- how many could you put on-line, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the time, but I could put all 1500 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, there came a time, from approximately the 11th of June, 1993, and at least for the remainder of 1993, you were the deputy commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, deputy to Mr. Blaskic; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what I asked you a few moments ago about the characteristics and responsibilities of a good deputy, and in fact you anticipated and answered my question perhaps somewhat, but during the time that you were a deputy to Mr. Blaskic, did you consider yourself a good officer and a responsible deputy to him?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On some of the documentation that the Judges may have seen through the months, there is sometimes an abbreviation "ONO." Can you explain what "ONO" stands for?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It dates back to Yugoslavia and would mean "total national defence," "All-People's Defence."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: ONO?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "All-People's Defence," or it could be an abbreviation for a place in the command at headquarters. Then it would be the operative -- the Operations and Training Department; so not an individual, but this body.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, there was an ONO officer or operations officer in each operations zone, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in Central Bosnia, were you considered not only the deputy, but also the operations -- the chief operations officer, or did somebody else hold that position?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Chief of Staff was Franjo Nakic. Blaskic was the commander. I was the deputy. The Chief of Staff was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness said "Blaskic."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the operations person -- officer was Marijan something, Marijan --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, perhaps we'll come to it. And during the time that you were the commander of the Travnik Brigade -- well, excuse me. My apologies. When you'd become the deputy commander to Blaskic from June 11, 19 -- well, earlier than that, actually. But during the time that you were deputy - excuse me for my hesitation - where was your duty station? Were you in his office in Vitez, were you in the same building in Vitez? Where were you located?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The deputy, well, his seat was in -- well, in 1992, at the beginning of 1992, there was a facility called "Lovac" where I established the headquarters in Vitez, and then Blaskic relocated it to Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And once you became his deputy, was that where your -- primarily once it moved to Hotel Vitez, was your office also at Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And approximately what proximity to Mr. Blaskic? I mean, were you next-door to each other, across the hall? How close was your office to Mr. Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was mostly just four to five metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And let me ask you a similar question to the one I asked you about the Travnik Brigade. On the Central Bosnia Operative Zone Command Staff, did you also have a daily or morning briefing?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
