utterances.text: No -- or, rather, I didn't -- well, there were briefings, yes, but not of any intensity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, how often were these briefings?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just stipulate what time the questions and answers relate to? What period are we dealing with?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For the time being, if I didn't say so - I thought I did - but I was talking from approximately 11 June 1993 to the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So can I get back to my question? So how often were these briefings or other meetings for the purposes of --

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prosecutor, you're not asking me precise questions, so I can't answer. You want a yes-or-no answer, but the question isn't precise enough. And then you won't allow me to expand. What I said was in June 1993, I spent days in the Travnik Brigade to deal with the situation. What deputy? No, just direct fighting, combat. But the time you're referring to, the months, I'll answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question stands, and it wasn't in this case a yes-or-no question. How often -- when were these briefings or meetings among the Central Bosnia Operative Zone Command Staff and approximately how often during the time from 11 June 1993 forward, to the end 1993?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The briefings were held twice a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and at the forward command post when we had to relocate, and that was in Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you also mentioned in your previous testimony this week that at some point in time operational groups were formed. Not operative zone, but within the operations zone, the zone itself was divided into operational groups, approximately four groups; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was from June 1992 right up until around October, so that's when we met as commanders of the operative groups once a week, at the Lovac facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies. When you say "October," sir, what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the structure of operational groups continued until at least November 1993; correct? It may have modified -- it may have had some modifications, but there continued to be a level of command called "operational groups" until at least November 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be precise and say until October 1992. I'm saying that because up until then I was able to reach the brigade commanders for a meeting within two or three days to report on my meeting with Blaskic. Now, after October, I was no longer able to do that because it was difficult to move around because of the conflict in Novi Travnik, so I couldn't reach the brigade commanders on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, whether you could easily reach them or not, there continued to be, until November 1993, at least, operational groups, correct, and Ivica Rajic, throughout this period, was the commander of the operational group based in Kiseljak; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was commander of the operative group in Kiseljak, yes. Now, whether his group functioned until November, I really can't say now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me just try to cut this a little bit short. If the Judges have seen and continue to see HVO documents from Central Bosnia describe an operational group based in Kiseljak that Mr. Rajic was in charge of, and when it says such things like "OG-2," you have no reason to disagree with me that that was Ivica Rajic; correct?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. How were General Blaskic's written orderings prepared? If General Blaskic gave an order, I want to send this unit, I want the brigade in Travnik to do something, I want the brigade in Busovaca to do something, and he wanted to prepare a written order, take us through the steps by which he would do that.

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blaskic would -- it would be his conception. He would write a large part of it, and then his staff would give shape to it in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, when you say "his staff would give shape to it," help us out a bit more. What particular staff would take his concept and then take it to the next level and then, presumably, transmit it in some way?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Franjo Nakic, or Slavko Marin. I've just remembered his surname, name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I agree with you, sir, Slavko Marin. And that was about orders. Well, how did it -- did someone then take it to a communications officer, to a duty officer? How does the -- how does the document then get from Hotel Vitez to the field?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, the order would then go to the Communications Centre to be sent off to those -- to whom it could be sent off to, and that was possible to almost all the brigades. You couldn't do it to Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let me ask a similar question. I was asking you about orders. Let me ask you about reports. In terms of reports that the operative zone had to send to the Main Staff, how were those reports prepared and transmitted?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports were prepared more regularly than the orders, and, in a way, they were regular, daily or weekly. And Blaskic, Nakic, Marin, the communications man --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was your role in connection with these documents, as deputy commander? As the number 2 man in the operative zone, what role did you play in the preparation of orders, the preparation of reports to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Requests for something to be stated more precisely. We would ask Blaskic at the briefing, and if something needed to be done, then I compiled it. But I didn't do that, in principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me -- it might be the last question we have time for this evening. Let me turn the other direction. The reports that came to the Central Bosnia Operative Zone from the subordinate units, either from the operational groups or lower down from the brigades, do you know how those were received and processed at Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the type of report, if it was directly from the commander, but once again the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's make it a bit more concrete, if that might help you. If a report was coming in, let's say, from the brigade in Busovaca, and reporting information about activities there, perhaps combat activities, presumably this is something that both you, as deputy, and Mr. Blaskic would want to know about?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the brigade commander, down to the military district, through the system of communications, the staff, the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Now I just want -- I'm being very, very basic here, sir, so we can understand some things. How did a report from the commander of the Busovaca Brigade get on Blaskic's desk? "Important matter. We think there's BiH troops coming this way." Blaskic, please give us some direction." Signed commander, Busovaca Brigade. How does that information get to Blaskic so that he can do something about it?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was like this: Niko Jozinovic and the brigade commander compiled a document, or rang up on the phone, or he solved the problem that faced him. He sent out the document in the same way that he received documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How did it get to Colonel Blaskic or to yourself? It doesn't do any good if it comes in, sir, and it sits in the communications -- in the duty officer's "out" box. How did it get to you or to Colonel Blaskic so that you -- either Colonel Blaskic or you, as the number 2 person, could actually do something about it, or did you not keep yourself informed?

utterances.speaker: FILIP FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not possible that I wasn't informed. I'm talking about the Communications Centre, the Operative Department, and then it reaches Blaskic. It is recorded by the recording clerk or whoever. But don't you think that the army -- or, rather, the HVO was an army as you would expect it to be on paper and everything else, given the circumstances? I don't know where your questions are leading, but, anyway, bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, for half an hour Mr. Scott has been asking very specific questions, very specific, and I thank him for that. Thanks to his questions, we can understand how things worked at the Hotel Vitez. These are straightforward questions. They're very specific, and you can answer, but you're not answering. I don't understand why you won't answer. He's doing everything he can to broach on the subject in a very neutral manner. He's saying, for example, Let's take the Busovaca Brigade, sending a report, what happens next? I mean, it's dead simple. All we want to know is if it's a packet transmission, it will arrive at a transmission centre and it will be recorded. This is what we want. Don't think that behind every question, be it a question from the Prosecution, the Judges, or the Defence, there's a trap. Absolutely not. You know, we want to know what's happening, we want to know what happened. If you're always, you know, thinking that there's going to be a trick behind the question, and if you're on your guard, you know, I understand why you won't answer, but these are straightforward questions. He's just asking you to say what happens, in practice, when a report arrives at the transmission centre, what happens. It's very simple. You're a general. I mean, a basic private could answer. I was a private at one point in time, and I managed, you know, to record this kind of documents and so on. And you were a general, so you must know what happened. And Mr. Scott absolutely wants to know about this. I'm sure he'll revisit this tomorrow, because as of now, we don't have the answer. At least I don't have the answer. But it's 7.00 p.m., it's time to stop, but we will resume tomorrow at 2.15. We'll have only one break, as I said, and we will stop for the week at 6.00 p.m. And I'm sure that we will resume next Monday, because we won't be done by tomorrow, 6.00 p.m. Well, anyway, have a pleasant evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 3rd day of December, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
